newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: NATO sees Russia, enlargement key to July summit.
newsitem.headline: NATO sees Russia, enlargement key to July summit.

text.p: NATO aims to lay the groundwork for enlargement, closer ties with Russia and a new command structure ahead of an alliance summit in Madrid in July, Secretary-General Javier Solana said on Thursday.

"These are the three key vectors of NATO's transformation. Up to now they have been developing in parallel. Our aim is to make them converge by the time of the summit in July," said Solana, who is on an official visit to Vienna, the first by a NATO secretary-general to neutral Austria.

In a speech to the association of Austrian industrialists, the former Spanish foreign minister sought to allay Russian fears of isolation and said he hoped eastward enlargement would be accompanied by historic new pacts with Russia and Ukraine.

"Any sober assessment of Russia's national interest leads one to the conclusion that a privileged relationship with the new NATO serves the new Russia better than a grudging retreat into self-isolation," he said.
"I am confident that this analysis will ultimately carry the day in Moscow and that by the summit we will have entered into a new, durable relationship," he added.
Solana visits Moscow on Monday for talks with Russian leaders.
He said the 16-member alliance also hoped to formalise its relationship with the Ukraine ahead of the July summit, which would contribute to greater European security.
"An enhanced relationship between NATO and Ukraine will help Ukraine to assume its rightful place as a confident partner and neighbour."

Solana reaffirmed NATO's commitment to enlargement to include former Warsaw Pact nations and said the organisation would invite the first countries to begin accession negotiations in July, with a view to joining by 1999.

"It is our historic obligation to respond to the new democracies of central and Eastern Europe... They deserve to be given the same chance that Western Europe was given after the Second World War," he said.
NATO's expansion would create the need for a stronger Partnership for Peace to involve countries that remained outside the organisation, Solana continued.
The Madrid summit would also put the finishing touches to NATO's new, smaller command structure and finalise plans for a greater European role outlined at NATO's meeting in Berlin last June.
